Let’s talk about something that’s often misunderstood— forgiveness.
This is Chapter Seven: Navigating Forgiveness—Letting Go Without Forgetting.
Now, a lot of people think forgiveness means excusing or forgetting a betrayal. But the truth is, forgiveness is really about you. It’s a personal process—one that frees you from the grip of resentment, even if the relationship itself never goes back to what it was.
Think of forgiveness like crossing a river. You don’t have to get across in one big leap. Instead, you step from stone to stone, taking it at your own pace.
So, what does that actually look like in real life?
First, it’s about acknowledging the full impact of what happened. Don’t brush aside your pain or try to convince yourself it wasn’t a big deal.
Next, let yourself feel all the emotions—anger, sadness, grief. There’s no need to bottle them up or pretend they’re not there.
And here’s something to remember: the betrayal isn’t a reflection of your worth. Separate what happened from how you see yourself. You’re not defined by someone else’s choices.
Forgiveness doesn’t have to mean you go back to how things were. You can choose to forgive for your own peace of mind, even if you decide the relationship can’t continue.
But if you do stay, know that forgiveness is a journey, not a destination. It unfolds over time, often alongside the slow rebuilding of trust.
Let me share a real-world example. Imagine a woman who’s spent months feeling angry and distant after being hurt. She starts to notice that carrying all that resentment is just exhausting. So, she sits down and writes a letter—not to send, but simply to get her feelings out and let go of the weight she’s been carrying.
That moment, when she allows herself to release the burden, can be a true turning point. It’s an act of self-forgiveness and opens up space for growth and healing.
So, if you find yourself holding onto old hurts, just remember—letting go doesn’t mean forgetting. It means choosing peace for yourself, one step at a time.
